en: Thus have I heard— Majjhima Nikāya 130, the Devadūta Sutta (The Discourse on the Divine Messengers).
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:

“Bhikkhus, suppose there were two houses with doors, and a man with sight standing in the middle of them were to see people entering the house, leaving the house, walking back and forth, and wandering about;”

In the same way, monks, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, I see beings passing away and being reborn—lowly and exalted, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate; I recognize beings according to their karma:
"These worthy beings, indeed, were possessed of good conduct of body and good conduct of speech..."
They were endowed with good conduct of mind, not revilers of the noble ones, possessing right view, and undertaking actions based on right view;
at the breaking up of the body, after death, they were reborn in a happy destination, a heavenly world.
Or else, these worthy beings were endowed with good conduct of body, endowed with good conduct of speech, and endowed with good conduct of mind.
They did not revile the noble ones, held right view, and undertook actions based on right view; with the breakup of the body, after death, they were reborn among human beings.
But these worthy beings, it seems, were possessed of misconduct of body, possessed of misconduct of speech, and possessed of misconduct of mind;
they reviled the noble ones, held wrong view, and undertook actions based on wrong view.
With the breakup of the body, after death, they were reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts. But these worthy beings, possessing misconduct of body,
possessing misconduct of speech, possessing misconduct of mind, revilers of the noble ones, holding wrong views,
and undertaking actions based on wrong views— with the breakup of the body, after death, were reborn in the womb of animals.
‘These worthy beings, however, were possessed of misconduct in body, misconduct in speech, and misconduct in mind;
they were revilers of the noble ones, held wrong views, and undertook actions based on wrong views.
With the breakup of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.’”
Then, monks, the wardens of hell seize him by his various limbs and present him to King Yama, saying:
“Sire, this man was disrespectful toward his mother, disrespectful toward his father, undisciplined toward recluses, undisciplined toward brahmins, and did not honor his elders in the family.
May Your Majesty inflict punishment upon him.”
Then, monks, King Yama questions, interrogates, and cross-examines him regarding that first divine messenger:
“O man, did you not see the first divine messenger appearing among humans?
He replies thus:
‘I did not see him, Bhante.
Then, monks, King Yama says to him:
‘Ho there, man! Did you not see among humans a young boy, tender and lying on his back, wallowing in his own urine and excrement?’”
He says thus:
"I saw them, Bhante.
To him, monks, King Yama says this:
“O man, did it never occur to you—that you were wise, mindful, and mature—to think:
‘I too am subject to birth; I have not transcended birth. Come now, let me do what is wholesome by way of body, speech, and mind’?
He replied thus:
‘I was not able, Bhante; I was negligent, Bhante.
To him, monks, King Yama says this:
‘O man, because of your negligence, you did not do what is good by way of body, speech, or mind.’
Truly, good man, they will deal with you exactly as one who is heedless deserves.
Moreover, this evil deed of yours was not done by your mother, nor by your father, nor by your brother,
nor by your sister, nor by your friends and companions, nor by your kinsmen and blood relations, nor by recluses and brahmins.

‘This was not done by your mother, nor by your father, nor by your brother, nor by your sister, nor by your friends and companions, nor by your relatives and kin, nor by deities, nor by ascetics and brahmins; this evil deed was done by you alone, and you yourself shall experience its result.
Then, monks, King Yama, having interrogated, examined, and reproached him regarding the first divine messenger, interrogates, examines, and reproaches him regarding the second divine messenger:
‘Ho there, man! Did you not see the second divine messenger appearing among human beings?’”
He says thus:
"I did not see him, Bhante.
To him, monks, King Yama speaks thus:
“O man, have you not seen among human beings a woman or a man who is aged, bent like a roof-rafter, crooked,
leaning on a staff for support, trembling as they walk, afflicted, their youth gone, with broken teeth,
grey hair, thinning hair, bald, wrinkled, and their body covered with age spots?”
He says thus:
‘I saw them, Bhante.
Then, monks, King Yama says this to him:
“O man, did it not occur to you—being wise, mindful, and elderly—‘I too am subject to old age;
I have not transcended old age. Come now, let me do what is wholesome by way of body, speech, and mind’?
He replied thus:
‘I was not able, Bhante; I was negligent, Bhante.
To him, monks, King Yama says this:
‘O man, because of your negligence you did not do what is wholesome by body, speech, or mind.’
Truly, good man, they will treat you exactly as one who is heedless deserves.
Furthermore, this evil deed of yours was not done by your mother, nor by your father, nor by your brother,
nor by your sister, nor by your friends and colleagues, nor by your kinsmen and relatives, nor by recluses and brahmins.

‘This was not done by your mother, nor by your father, nor by your brother, nor by your sister, nor by your friends and companions, nor by your relatives and kin, nor by deities; this evil deed was done by you alone, and you yourself shall experience its result.
Then, monks, King Yama, having questioned, examined, and exhorted him regarding the second divine messenger, questions, examines, and exhorts him regarding the third divine messenger:
‘Ho there, man! Did you not see the third divine messenger appearing among human beings?’
He says thus:
‘I did not see them, Bhante.
Then, monks, King Yama says this to him:

“O man, have you not seen among human beings a woman or a man who is afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill, lying fouled in their own urine and excrement, being lifted up by some and laid down by others?
He replied:
“I have seen them, venerable sir.”
Then, monks, King Yama said to him:
"O man, it did not occur to you—though you were wise, mature, and discerning—that 'I too am subject to illness; I am not exempt from illness.'"
‘Well then, I shall do what is wholesome by way of body, speech, and mind. He replies:
‘I will not be able to, Bhante; I might be negligent, Bhante.
Then, monks, King Yama says this to him:
“O man, through negligence you have done what is unwholesome by way of body, speech, and mind.
Truly, O man, they will deal with you according to that negligence.
Furthermore, this evil deed of yours was not done by your mother, nor by your father, nor by your brother.”
‘Sister, this was not done by your sister, nor by your friends and companions, nor by your kinsmen and blood relations, nor by recluses and brahmins, nor by the deities;
rather, this evil deed was done by you yourself, and you alone shall experience its result.
Monks, after King Yama has thus interrogated, examined, and exhorted him regarding the third divine messenger, he interrogates, examines, and exhorts him regarding the fourth divine messenger:
“O man, did you not see the fourth divine messenger appearing among human beings?
He replied:
“I did not see him, Bhante.”
Then, monks, King Yama says to him:

“Ho there, man! Did you not see among humans when kings, having seized a thief or a wrongdoer, inflict various punishments upon them—beating them with whips, beating them with canes, beating them with split bamboo, or cutting off their hands, or their feet?”
Whether they cut off his hands and feet, or cut off his ears, or cut off his nose, or cut off both his ears and nose,
or subject him to the *bilaṅgathālika* torture, or subject him to the *saṅkhamuṇḍika* torture, or subject him to the *rāhumukha* torture, or subject him to the *jotimālika* torture,
or subject him to the *hatthapajjotika* torture, or subject him to the *erakavattika* torture, or subject him to the *cīrakavāsika* torture.
"Are they doing the 'antelope' torture, the 'fish-hook' torture, the 'coin' torture, the 'caustic-liquid-and-bark-scraping' torture,
the 'rolling-pin' torture, the 'straw-mat' torture, pouring boiling oil over them, having them devoured by dogs,
impaling them alive on stakes, or cutting off their heads with swords?"
He says thus:
“I saw them, venerable sir.
Then, monks, King Yama says this to him:

“O man, did it not occur to you—a wise and mature person—‘It seems, sir, that those who perform evil deeds undergo such various punishments for their actions even in this very life, so what need is there to mention the next world? Come now, let me do good with body, speech, and mind’?
He replied thus:
‘I was not able, Bhante; I was negligent, Bhante.
Then, monks, King Yama says to him:
‘O man, because of your negligence, you have done no good with body, speech, or mind.’
"Truly, good man, they will deal with you exactly as one who is heedless deserves.
Furthermore, this evil deed of yours was not done by your mother, nor by your father, nor by your brother,
nor by your sister, nor by your friends and companions, nor by your kinsmen and blood relations, nor by recluses and brahmins."

‘This was not done by your mother, nor by your father, nor by your brother, nor by your sister, nor by your friends and companions, nor by your relatives and kin, nor by deities, nor by ascetics and brahmins; this evil deed was done by you alone, and you alone shall experience its result.
Then, monks, after King Yama has questioned, examined, and reproached him regarding the fourth divine messenger, he questions, examines, and reproaches him regarding the fifth divine messenger:
‘Ho there, man! Did you not see the fifth divine messenger appearing among human beings?’
He says thus:
"I did not see him, Bhante.
To him, monks, King Yama speaks thus:
“O man, have you not seen among human beings a woman or a man dead for one day, or dead for two days, or dead for three days—swollen, discolored, and festering?
He replied:
“I have seen them, venerable sir.”
Then, monks, King Yama says this to him:
“O man, did it not occur to you—you who were wise, mature, and discerning—that ‘I too am subject to death;
I have not transcended death. Come now, let me do what is wholesome by way of body, speech, and mind’?”
He speaks thus:
"I was not able, Bhante; I was negligent, Bhante.
To him, monks, King Yama says this:
“O man, through negligence you have not done what is good by way of body, speech, or mind.
Truly, O man, they will deal with you according to that negligence.
Furthermore, this evil deed of yours was not done by your mother, nor by your father, nor by your brother.”
‘This was not done by your sister, nor by your friends and colleagues, nor by your kinsmen and blood relations, nor by recluses and brahmins, nor by the deities;
this evil deed was done by you alone, and you alone shall experience its result.
Monks, having thus questioned, examined, and exhorted him regarding the fifth divine messenger, King Yama falls silent.
Then, monks, the wardens of hell inflict upon him a form of torture called the fivefold binding:
they thrust a red-hot iron stake through one hand, they thrust a red-hot iron stake through the other hand,
they thrust a red-hot iron stake through one foot, they thrust a red-hot iron stake through the other foot, and they thrust a red-hot iron stake through the middle of his chest.
There he experiences painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter sensations, yet he does not die as long as that evil karma has not been exhausted.
Then, monks, the wardens of hell lay him down and pare him with axes...
[as before] ...Then, monks, the wardens of hell seize him by his feet and hold him upside down, head downwards, and pare him with adzes... [as before] ...
“Monks, the wardens of hell yoke that person to a chariot and drive him back and forth across ground that is burning, blazing, and aflame...
Monks, the wardens of hell make that person climb up and down a great mountain of glowing coals that is burning, blazing, and aflame...
Monks, the wardens of hell seize that person by his feet and head, and cast him into a cauldron of molten iron that is heated, blazing, and aflame.”
There he is cooked in a mass of froth.
While being cooked there in that mass of froth, he goes up at one time, down at another, and across at another.
There he experiences painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter sensations; yet he does not die as long as that evil karma has not been exhausted.
Then, monks, the wardens of hell throw him into the Great Hell.
Now, monks, that Great Hell has four corners and four gates.
Divided into sections and measured out by parts,
it is surrounded by an iron wall and closed in with iron.
For him, there is a ground made of iron,
blazing and filled with heat,
extending for a hundred yojanas on all sides.
It remains pervading [them] at all times.
Furthermore, monks, the flames rising from the eastern wall of that Great Hell strike against the western wall;
the flames rising from the western wall strike against the eastern wall.
Flames rising from the northern wall strike against the southern wall;
flames rising from the southern wall strike against the northern wall; flames rising from below strike upwards;
and flames rising from above strike downwards.
Thus, there he experiences feelings that are painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter; yet he does not die as long as that evil karma has not been exhausted.
There comes a time, monks, when after the lapse of a very long period, the eastern gate of that great hell is opened.
He then runs toward it with swift speed.
As he runs with swift speed, his outer skin burns, his inner skin burns, his flesh burns, his sinews burn, and even his bones emit smoke;
yet it remains exactly as it was before. But when he has reached the full measure of his suffering, monks, then that door is closed.
There he experiences painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter sensations, yet he does not die until that evil karma has been exhausted.
There comes a time, monks, when after the lapse of a long period, the western gate of that great hell is opened...
the northern gate is opened...
the southern gate is opened.
Thus, he runs there with great speed.
As he runs with that great speed, his outer skin burns, his inner skin burns, his flesh burns, his sinews burn, and even his bones emit smoke; yet what has been torn away remains exactly as it was.
But when he has reached the full extent [of the path], monks, then that door is closed.
There he experiences painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter sensations, yet he does not die as long as that evil karma has not been exhausted.
There comes a time, monks, when after the lapse of a very long period, the eastern gate of that great hell is opened.
He then runs toward it with swift speed.
As he runs with great speed, his outer skin burns, his inner skin burns, his flesh burns, his sinews burn, and even his bones emit smoke; yet when it is pulled away, it is exactly as before.
He exits through that gate.
Now, monks, immediately adjacent to that Great Hell is the Great Feces Hell.
Thus it falls there.
And in that Excrement Hell, monks, needle-mouthed creatures cut through the outer skin; having cut through the outer skin, they cut through the inner skin;
having cut through the inner skin, they cut through the flesh; having cut through the flesh, they cut through the sinews.
Having cut through the sinews, they cut through the bones; having cut through the bones, they eat the marrow.
There he experiences painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter sensations, yet he does not die as long as that evil karma has not been exhausted.
Immediately adjacent to that Excrement Hell, monks, is the great Hell of Embers.
Thus he falls there.
There he experiences painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter sensations, yet he does not die as long as that evil karma has not been exhausted.
Immediately adjacent to that Kukkula hell, monks, is a great forest of *simbali* trees, rising a league high, with thorns sixteen finger-breadths long, burning, blazing, and glowing.
There they are both raised up and cast down.
There he experiences painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter sensations, yet he does not die until that evil kamma has been exhausted.
Immediately adjacent to that *simbali* forest, monks, is a vast forest of sword-leaves.
Thus he enters there.
Its leaves, stirred by the wind, fall and cut off his hand, cut off his foot, cut off both his hands and feet, cut off his ear, cut off his nose, and cut off both his ears and nose.
There he experiences painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter sensations; yet he does not die so long as that evil karma has not been exhausted.
"Furthermore, monks, immediately adjacent to that Forest of Sword-leaves is a great river of caustic water.
There he falls;
there he is carried along with the current, against the current, and both with and against the current."
There he experiences painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter sensations, yet he does not die as long as that evil karma has not been exhausted.
Then, monks, the wardens of hell pull him out with a hook, place him on dry land, and say to him:
"O man, what do you desire?"
He speaks thus:
“I am hungry, venerable sir.
Then, monks, the wardens of hell pry open his mouth with a red-hot iron hook—blazing, flaming, and glowing—and they thrust into his mouth a red-hot iron ball—blazing, flaming, and glowing.
Thus it burns his lips, it burns his mouth, it burns his throat, it burns his chest, and having taken up his intestines and mesentery, it exits through the lower part of the body.
There he experiences painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter sensations; yet he does not die as long as that evil karma has not been exhausted.
Then, monks, the wardens of hell say this to him:
“O man, what do you desire? He replied,
“I am thirsty, venerable sir.”
Then, monks, the wardens of hell force open his mouth with a red-hot iron hook—blazing, flaming, and glowing—and pour into his mouth molten copper that is blazing, flaming, and glowing.
It burns his lips, it burns his mouth, it burns his throat, it burns his chest, and having consumed the intestines and the mesentery, it passes out through the lower part of the body.
Thus, there he experiences painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter sensations, yet he does not die as long as that evil karma has not been exhausted.
Then, monks, the wardens of hell throw him back again into the Great Hell.
Once in the past, monks, this thought occurred to King Yama:
‘Indeed, sirs, those who commit evil, unwholesome deeds in the world are subjected to such various punishments.
Oh, that I might obtain human birth! And that a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, might arise in the world! And that I might attend upon that Blessed One.
And that the Blessed One might teach me the Dhamma. And that I might understand the Dhamma of that Blessed One.’”
“Furthermore, monks, I do not say this having heard it from another ascetic or brahmin; rather, I say only that which has been known by myself, seen by myself, and realized by myself.
This is what the Blessed One said.
Having said this, the Sublime One, the Teacher, further said this:
“Those young men who are heedless and are rebuked by the messengers of the gods,
they grieve for a long time.”
Those men who go to an inferior state,
and those virtuous, true persons here who [are guided] by the messengers of the gods;
Urged on, they never at any time neglect the noble Dhamma,
seeing danger in grasping.
In the occurrence of birth and death,
they are liberated through non-clinging,
in the destruction of birth and death.
Having attained security, they are happy,
extinguished in this very life;
having transcended all enmity and fear, they dwell at peace.
“He has transcended all suffering.
The *Devadūta Sutta* is finished, the tenth.
The third chapter, the *Suññatavagga*, is finished.
Its summary verse:
Emptiness is twofold, the marvelous quality,
and the Bākula story.
The Aciravatī, the Bhūmi, the Janavasabha,
the Anuruddha, the Upakkilesa,
the Bālapaṇḍita, and the Devadūta— these are the ten.
